title: Veterans Health Administration cluster-randomized rollout of GI Genius: adenoma detection rises from 50.7% to 54.9% at equipped facilities
summary: At 42 VA facilities chosen at random to receive GI Genius, adenoma detection rose from 50.7% to 54.9%, while it fell from 51.8% to 51.1% at 97 control facilities.
account: The National Gastroenterology and Hepatology Program of the Veterans Health Administration ran a pragmatic cluster-randomized quality improvement study of computer-aided polyp detection in the United States. Between October 2022 and February 2023 the program equipped randomly selected VA facilities with the devices; the trial registry names the device as the GI Genius Intelligent Endoscopy Module from Medtronic. Control facilities were given a random deployment date for comparison. The analysis covered 269 endoscopists at 42 equipped facilities, who performed 71,594 colonoscopies before deployment and 35,399 after, and 547 endoscopists at 97 control facilities, who performed 151,792 before and 75,415 after. At the equipped facilities the adenoma detection rate rose from 50.7% to 54.9%, an absolute increase of 4.2 percentage points. At the control facilities it fell from 51.8% to 51.1%. In a regression model, availability of the device was associated with 22% higher odds of adenoma detection. The device did not change the detection of other lesions or the withdrawal time. The authors state that the effect on cancer outcomes and the risk that endoscopists lose skill remain unknown.
purpose: GI Genius was built to flag possible polyps on the colonoscopy video in real time. The higher adenoma detection was that purpose.
deployer: Veterans Health Administration, National Gastroenterology and Hepatology Program

ratings.reason: More veterans had precancerous adenomas found and removed: detection rose from 50.7% to 54.9% of colonoscopies at equipped facilities.
The VA raised a core colonoscopy quality measure by 4.2 percentage points without a change in withdrawal time.

brief: The Veterans Health Administration tested computer-aided polyp detection in routine colonoscopy at scale.[1] It assigned facilities at random to receive a polyp-detection device, which the trial registry names as Medtronic's GI Genius. At 42 equipped facilities adenoma detection rose from 50.7% to 54.9%. At 97 control facilities it fell from 51.8% to 51.1%. Withdrawal time did not change. The gain was 4.2 percentage points on a baseline that was already about 51%. The rate of 54.9% rests on 35,399 colonoscopies. The Veterans Health Administration program that installed the devices also ran and reported the study.[2] The authors state that the effect on cancer outcomes remains unknown, as does the risk that endoscopists lose skill. Elsewhere, researchers found a gain in a randomized trial at two Seoul hospitals and no gain in another at a Japanese community hospital.
